question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

INTREPID
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Fearless.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Intrepid (adjective) means showing no fear in the face of danger or difficulty; resolutely courageous. (निडर, निर्भीक)
◦ Example: The intrepid climbers reached the summit despite the blizzard.

 

• Fearless carries precisely this sense — without fear, bold and undaunted. (निर्भीक)
◦ Example: She was a fearless reporter who filed stories from the war zone.

 

• The word is formed from Latin in- (not) + trepidus (alarmed, agitated) — literally “not trembling”. The same root survives in trepidation (a feeling of fear about something that may happen).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Timid (डरपोक, संकोची): lacking courage and easily frightened — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 2: Cautious (सावधान): careful to avoid danger; not fearful, but certainly not intrepid.

 

• Option 4: Anxious (चिंतित, बेचैन): worried and uneasy about what may happen.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of intrepid asked in SSC: dauntless, valiant, undaunted, audacious, gallant.

 

• Antonyms: cowardly, craven, timorous, faint-hearted, pusillanimous.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To bell the cat
option_1: To warn others of a hidden danger
option_2: To undertake a risky task for the good of all
option_3: To raise a false alarm deliberately
option_4: To win favour by flattering a superior
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To undertake a risky task for the good of all.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To bell the cat” means to take on a dangerous or difficult task on behalf of a group, especially one that everybody agrees is necessary but nobody is willing to attempt. (खतरे का काम सबके लिए अपने जिम्मे लेना)
◦ Example: Everyone wanted the decision reversed, but nobody was ready to bell the cat before the board.

 

• The idiom comes from the old fable in which the mice agree that a bell round the cat’s neck would save them all — until one asks the fatal question: who will tie it on?

 

• Note the emphasis on doing, not merely on warning; the mice already knew the danger. That is what separates the correct option from the first distractor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes giving a warning, for which one would say “to sound the alarm”.

 

• Option 3 describes a false alarm — “to cry wolf”.

 

• Option 4 describes flattery — “to curry favour” or “to butter someone up”.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of courage frequently set alongside it: to take the bull by the horns, to stick one’s neck out, to put one’s head on the block, to face the music.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

AUGMENT
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Diminish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Augment (verb) means to make something greater by adding to it; to increase in size, amount or value. (बढ़ाना, वृद्धि करना)
◦ Example: He augmented his salary by teaching in the evenings.

 

• Diminish means to make or become smaller or less, and is therefore its direct opposite. (घटाना, कम करना)
◦ Example: The steady rain diminished the intensity of the fire.

 

• The word comes from Latin augere (to increase) — the same root as auction (a sale in which bids keep rising) and augmentation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Increase (बढ़ाना): to make greater — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Expand (फैलाना): to become larger in size or scope — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Enlarge (बड़ा करना): to make bigger — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• When three options agree and one stands apart, the odd option is the answer in an antonym question. Other antonyms of augment: curtail, abate, reduce, dwindle, contract.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Independant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is INDEPENDENT, ending in -ent, not -ant. It means not controlled or influenced by others; self-governing. (स्वतंत्र)
◦ Example: The inquiry was conducted by an independent committee.

 

• Fix it through the family: depend → dependent → independent, and the noun independence — all with e. A useful memory aid is that independence is spelt with an e in the same place as excellence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Liaison (संपर्क, समन्वय): communication or cooperation between groups — correctly spelt, with two ‘i’s (li-ai-son).

 

• Option 2: Pronunciation (उच्चारण): the way a word is spoken — correctly spelt. Note that it is pronunciation, although the verb is pronounce.

 

• Option 4: Recommend (सिफारिश करना): to advise or put forward as suitable — correctly spelt, with a single ‘c’ and double ‘m’.

 

NOTE

 

• The -ent / -ant pair is a standing SSC trap. With e: independent, existent, persistent, consistent, competent. With a: relevant, resistant, assistant, abundant, defiant.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the adjective meaning ‘impossible to satisfy’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Insatiable.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Insatiable (adjective) means impossible to satisfy, however much is given. (अतृप्त, अतृप्तिकर)
◦ Example: The child had an insatiable curiosity about how machines worked.

 

• The spelling follows from the root: Latin satiare (to satisfy) with the negative prefix in-, giving in + sati + able. The related words satiate, satiety and satisfy all keep the -sati- sequence with a t, never a c.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Insatiabale — an extra ‘a’ has been inserted in the ending; the suffix is simply -able.

 

• Option 3: Insaciable — the ‘c’ wrongly replaces the ‘t’ of the root satiare.

 

• Option 4: Insatieable — a spurious ‘e’ has crept in before -able.

 

NOTE

 

• Adjectives of this pattern are tested often: inevitable, irreparable, indispensable, irresistible, incorrigible. Note that some take -able and others -ible; there is no shortcut except to learn them in pairs.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

 ‘A remedy supposed to cure all diseases and difficulties’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Panacea.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A panacea is a supposed cure for every disease or for every difficulty; a universal remedy. (रामबाण औषधि, सर्वरोगनाशक)
◦ Example: Higher spending is no panacea for the problems of the health system.

 

• The word comes from Greek pan (all) + akos (cure), the name of Panacea, daughter of Asclepius, the goddess of universal remedy. The prefix pan- appears again in pandemic, panorama and pantheon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Placebo (नकली दवा): a harmless substance given in place of medicine, chiefly for its psychological effect or as a control in trials.

 

• Option 3: Antidote (मारक विष का प्रतिकारक): a medicine that counteracts a particular poison — specific, not universal.

 

• Option 4: Anodyne (पीड़ानाशक): something that relieves pain, or, as an adjective, something deliberately inoffensive.

 

NOTE

 

• The four options here are near neighbours in meaning, which is exactly how SSC frames such questions. Read the definition for its scope: all diseases points unmistakably to panacea.

question:
Select the correct option:

 

The revised guidelines are not consistent ____ the circular issued last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective consistent is always followed by the preposition with when it means in agreement with something else.
◦ Complete sentence: The revised guidelines are not consistent with the circular issued last year.
◦ Example: His account of the incident was consistent with the CCTV footage.

 

• Such combinations are fixed by usage, not by logic; they must be learnt as adjective + preposition units.

 

• Note the contrasting sense of the same word: consistent in is used for a person’s steady behaviour — She is consistent in her effort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘to’ follows adjectives such as similar, contrary, prior, liable, subordinate.

 

• Option 2: ‘for’ follows eligible, famous, eager, responsible, suitable.

 

• Option 4: ‘at’ follows good, bad, adept, expert, surprised — none of which fits here.

 

NOTE

 

• High-frequency pairs for SSC: conform to, comply with, accompanied by, deprived of, devoid of, averse to, indifferent to, acquainted with, endowed with.

question:
Select the correct option:

 

If the temperature ____ below zero, the water in the pipes freezes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. falls.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The main clause is in the simple present (freezes) and states a general truth — something that happens every time the condition is met. This is the zero conditional, whose structure is:
◦ If + simple present, … simple present.

 

• The blank therefore takes falls, agreeing with the singular subject the temperature.
◦ Complete sentence: If the temperature falls below zero, the water in the pipes freezes.

 

• The zero conditional is used for scientific facts, rules and habits; the word if here can be replaced by when or whenever without changing the sense — a quick test for identifying it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘fell’ belongs to the second conditional, which needs would in the main clause: If the temperature fell, the water would freeze.

 

• Option 3: ‘had fallen’ belongs to the third conditional, used for unreal past situations.

 

• Option 4: ‘would fall’ cannot be used in the if-clause of a conditional sentence at all.

 

NOTE

 

• The four conditionals at a glance: zero (if + present, present — facts); first (if + present, will + V1 — likely future); second (if + past, would + V1 — unlikely present); third (if + past perfect, would have + V3 — unreal past).

question:
Select the correct option:

 

Although the witness spoke with great confidence, several inconsistencies in his statement ____ his account.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. discredited.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence opens with “Although”, which signals a contrast. Confidence in the manner of speaking is set against something negative in the substance — so the blank must carry a sense of weakening or destroying belief.

 

• Discredit (verb) means to harm the good reputation of something or to cause it to be disbelieved. (अविश्वसनीय बनाना, साख गिराना)
◦ Example: The forged receipts discredited the entire claim.

 

• The subject of the blank is inconsistencies, which by their nature damage credibility — a second clue pointing to the same answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Corroborated (पुष्टि करना): to confirm or support with further evidence — the opposite of what inconsistencies do.

 

• Option 3: Vindicated (निर्दोष सिद्ध करना): to clear of blame or prove right.

 

• Option 4: Endorsed (समर्थन करना): to declare public approval of something.

 

NOTE

 

• In such fill-in-the-blank questions, first identify the connective — although, despite, yet, however demand a contrast, while because, since, therefore, hence demand agreement. The connective usually decides the answer before the vocabulary does.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The scheme was designed not only to reduce industrial waste (1)/ but also for increasing (2)/ the efficiency of the plant (3)/ within a period of two years. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correlative conjunction ‘not only … but also’ requires that the two elements it joins be of the same grammatical form — the rule of parallelism.

 

• The first element is the infinitive ‘to reduce’, so the second must also be an infinitive: ‘to increase’, not the prepositional phrase for increasing.
◦ Corrected: The scheme was designed not only to reduce industrial waste but also to increase the efficiency of the plant within a period of two years.

 

• A quick check: whatever word follows not only must be matched by the same kind of word after but also — verb with verb, noun with noun, phrase with phrase.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: not only to reduce industrial waste is a well-formed infinitive phrase.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the efficiency of the plant is the object of the second infinitive.

 

• Part (4) is correct: within a period of two years is an appropriate adverbial of time.

 

NOTE

 

• The correlative pairs must never be broken or mixed: not only … but also, either … or, neither … nor, both … and, whether … or, no sooner … than, scarcely … when.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

Each of the applicants (1)/ who were shortlisted last week (2)/ have been asked to appear (3)/ for a personal interview on Monday. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the main verb is ‘Each’, and each is always singular, however many people follow it. The verb must therefore be has been asked, not have been asked.
◦ Corrected: Each of the applicants who were shortlisted last week has been asked to appear for a personal interview on Monday.

 

• The plural noun applicants sits inside the prepositional phrase of the applicants and cannot govern the main verb. The relative clause who were shortlisted, however, correctly takes a plural verb, because who here refers to applicants, not to each.

 

• That contrast is the whole point of the question: two verbs, two different subjects in the same sentence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: Each of the applicants is a standard construction.

 

• Part (2) is correct: the plural were agrees with who, which stands for applicants.

 

• Part (4) is correct: an ordinary prepositional phrase of purpose and time.

 

NOTE

 

• Always singular: each, every, either, neither, one of, none (traditionally), everyone, somebody, nobody, each one. Always plural: both, few, several, many.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

The committee should review the safety guidelines before the monsoon.
option_1: The safety guidelines should have been reviewed by the committee before the monsoon.
option_2: The safety guidelines should be reviewed by the committee before the monsoon.
option_3: The safety guidelines are to be reviewed by the committee before the monsoon.
option_4: The safety guidelines must be being reviewed by the committee before the monsoon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The safety guidelines should be reviewed by the committee before the monsoon.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence contains a modal auxiliary (can, may, must, should, will, would), the passive is formed as:
◦ Object + modal + be + V3 + by + subject.

 

• Applying it here:
◦ the object the safety guidelines becomes the subject;
◦ should review becomes should be reviewed;
◦ the committee moves to the end with by;
◦ the adverbial before the monsoon stays where it is.

 

• The modal itself is never changed in the passive — should remains should, may remains may.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses should have been reviewed, the passive of the perfect modal should have reviewed, which suggests a duty already neglected.

 

• Option 3 replaces the modal with are to be, changing an obligation into a scheduled arrangement.

 

• Option 4 substitutes must for should and adds an ungrammatical continuous form.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare the two modal patterns: modal + be + V3 (The file may be sent today) and modal + have been + V3 (The file may have been sent yesterday). The first looks forward, the second looks back.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The treaty required both sides to lay down their arms.
option_1: He folded his arms and waited in silence.
option_2: The rebels refused to surrender their arms to the police.
option_3: The smuggling of arms across the border continued unchecked.
option_4: The country spends a fortune on arms every year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He folded his arms and waited in silence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but a wholly different meaning. In the given sentence, arms means weapons. (हथियार)

 

• In Option 1, arms refers to the two upper limbs of the body. (बाहें, भुजाएँ) That is an entirely different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The other three options all use arms in the sense of weapons, exactly as the highlighted word does, and so cannot be the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: surrender their arms — weapons; identical in meaning to the given sentence.

 

• Option 3: smuggling of arms — again weapons.

 

• Option 4: spends a fortune on arms — military equipment, the same sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the idioms built on both senses: to take up arms (to begin fighting), up in arms (angry and protesting), to welcome with open arms (to receive warmly), at arm’s length (at a distance).

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The files had been removed from the cabinet by someone before the audit began.
option_1: Someone removed the files from the cabinet before the audit began.
option_2: Someone had removed the files from the cabinet before the audit began.
option_3: The cabinet had removed the files before the audit began.
option_4: Someone has removed the files from the cabinet before the audit began.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Someone had removed the files from the cabinet before the audit began.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — someone — becomes the subject in the active voice, and the passive subject the files becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb had been removed is in the past perfect, so the active verb must also be past perfect → had removed. The past perfect is essential here, since it marks the action as earlier than the audit began.
◦ Active: Someone had removed the files from the cabinet before the audit began.

 

• Rule for perfect tenses: had been + V3 (passive) ↔ had + V3 (active); the auxiliary been disappears.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the simple past, which loses the sequence of the two past actions.

 

• Option 3 makes the cabinet the doer, which reverses the sense of the sentence.

 

• Option 4 uses the present perfect, which cannot be combined with the past clause before the audit began.

 

NOTE

 

• When the agent is a vague word such as someone, people, they, it may be dropped in the passive (The files had been removed before the audit began); but when converting to the active voice, the agent must be restored as the subject.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

The circular economy has moved from the margins of environmental debate to the centre of industrial planning. Where the conventional ‘linear’ model follows a straight line — extract, manufacture, use, discard — the circular model treats waste as a design failure rather than an inevitability. Products are conceived so that their components can be repaired, refurbished, remanufactured or, at the last, returned to the material stream from which they came. The ambition is not merely to recycle more efficiently, but to postpone the moment of disposal for as long as economic and physical life allows. The distinction matters, because recycling alone is often mistaken for circularity. Melting a metal casing down consumes fresh energy and degrades the material a little at every cycle; keeping the same casing in service through repair preserves both the energy and the value already embedded in it. Genuine circularity is therefore judged by a hierarchy — retain, repair, reuse, remanufacture, and only then recycle. Policy has begun to follow. Several jurisdictions now impose extended producer responsibility, obliging manufacturers to bear the cost of collecting and treating their goods at the end of their life; others have legislated a right to repair, requiring that spare parts, manuals and diagnostic tools be made available to independent workshops. Such rules do not by themselves create a circular economy, but they alter the arithmetic a firm uses at the drawing board, where the decisive choices about repairability are in fact made. Consumers exert a quieter pressure of their own. Once buyers began to ask how long a device would last and what it would cost to mend, durability acquired a market value it had previously lacked, and the marketing of disposability grew harder to sustain. The ultimate test of a society, then, is not how much it manages to recycle, but how little it needs to.

 

What does the author primarily convey about the circular economy?
option_1: It is simply a new name for recycling
option_2: It requires waste to be designed out and products to be kept in use for as long as possible
option_3: It has been rejected by industry as impractical
option_4: It applies only to metal products
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It requires waste to be designed out and products to be kept in use for as long as possible.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The opening lines set the circular model against the linear one and state its central idea: waste is treated as a design failure rather than an inevitability.

 

• The author then makes the aim explicit — the ambition is not merely to recycle more efficiently but to postpone the moment of disposal for as long as economic and physical life allows. That is precisely what the correct option states.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 states the confusion the passage explicitly warns against — recycling alone is mistaken for circularity.

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by the first sentence, which places the idea at the centre of industrial planning.

 

• Option 4 takes the passing example of a metal casing and turns it into the scope of the whole idea.

 

NOTE

 

• For “primarily conveys” questions, the answer is normally traceable to the opening or closing lines, where an expository passage states its thesis. Options built on a single illustration are too narrow.

Which action best reflects genuine circularity as described in the passage?
option_1: Melting down a metal casing to make a fresh one
option_3: Repairing a casing so that it stays in service
option_4: Exporting used goods to another country
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Repairing a casing so that it stays in service.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage supplies the comparison directly: melting a casing down consumes fresh energy and degrades the material at every cycle, whereas keeping the same casing in service through repair preserves both the energy and the value already embedded in it.

 

• The hierarchy given in the passage settles the matter — retain, repair, reuse, remanufacture, and only then recycle. Repair stands near the top; recycling is the last resort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is recycling, which the passage places at the bottom of the hierarchy.

 

• Option 2 concerns waste collection, which does nothing to keep a product in use.

 

• Option 4 is not discussed in the passage at all.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage supplies an explicit ranking or hierarchy, expect a question on it. Mark the order while reading; the answer is usually the item highest on the list.

How does the author distinguish recycling from genuine circularity?
option_1: By the cost borne by the consumer
option_2: By the loss of energy and embedded value at every cycle
option_3: By the involvement of the government
option_4: By the size of the manufacturing firm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. By the loss of energy and embedded value at every cycle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The distinction is drawn in a single sentence of comparison: melting the casing consumes fresh energy and degrades the material a little at every cycle, while repair preserves both the energy and the value already embedded in the object.

 

• Recycling is thus presented not as wrong but as costly and second-best — which is why the author calls it the last step of the hierarchy rather than the goal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is never mentioned; the passage speaks of energy and value, not of price to the buyer.

 

• Option 3 confuses this question with the later discussion of policy.

 

• Option 4 introduces the size of firms, which the passage nowhere considers.

 

NOTE

 

• “How does the author distinguish X from Y” questions are answered by the sentence in which both terms appear together. Locate that sentence instead of recalling the passage as a whole.

The ultimate test of a society, then, is not how much it manages to recycle, but how little it needs to.

 

According to the passage, what is the role of legislation in the circular economy?
option_1: It creates a circular economy entirely by itself
option_2: It bans the manufacture of new goods
option_3: It changes the calculation a firm makes while designing a product
option_4: It removes the need for consumer awareness
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. It changes the calculation a firm makes while designing a product.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage names two legal instruments — extended producer responsibility (the manufacturer must bear the cost of collecting and treating goods at the end of life) and the right to repair (spare parts, manuals and diagnostic tools must be available to independent workshops).

 

• It then states their limit and their real effect: such rules do not by themselves create a circular economy, but they alter the arithmetic a firm uses at the drawing board, where the decisive choices about repairability are made.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is denied word for word by the passage.

 

• Option 2 overstates the law; nothing is banned, only costed differently.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the following section, in which consumer pressure is given a role of its own.

 

NOTE

 

• Beware of options that convert a qualified claim (“not by themselves, but …”) into an absolute one. SSC uses this device in almost every comprehension passage.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

The circular economy has moved from the margins of environmental debate to the centre of industrial planning. Where the conventional ‘linear’ model follows a straight line — extract, manufacture, use, discard — the circular model treats waste as a design failure rather than an inevitability. Products are conceived so that their components can be repaired, refurbished, remanufactured or, at the last, returned to the material stream from which they came. The ambition is not merely to recycle more efficiently, but to postpone the moment of disposal for as long as economic and physical life allows. The distinction matters, because recycling alone is often mistaken for circularity. Melting a metal casing down consumes fresh energy and degrades the material a little at every cycle; keeping the same casing in service through repair preserves both the energy and the value already embedded in it. Genuine circularity is therefore judged by a hierarchy — retain, repair, reuse, remanufacture, and only then recycle. Policy has begun to follow. Several jurisdictions now impose extended producer responsibility, obliging manufacturers to bear the cost of collecting and treating their goods at the end of their life; others have legislated a right to repair, requiring that spare parts, manuals and diagnostic tools be made available to independent workshops. Such rules do not by themselves create a circular economy, but they alter the arithmetic a firm uses at the drawing board, where the decisive choices about repairability are in fact made. Consumers exert a quieter pressure of their own. Once buyers began to ask how long a device would last and what it would cost to mend, durability acquired a market value it had previously lacked, and the marketing of disposability grew harder to sustain. The ultimate test of a society, then, is not how much it manages to recycle, but how little it needs to.

 

Why does the author consider consumers important to this shift?
option_1: Because their demand for long-lasting goods gives durability a market value
option_2: Because they finance the building of recycling plants
option_3: Because they take part in designing new products
option_4: Because they oppose government regulation of industry
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Because their demand for long-lasting goods gives durability a market value.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage says that once buyers began to ask how long a device would last and what it would cost to mend, durability acquired a market value it had previously lacked, and the marketing of disposability became harder to sustain.

 

• The pressure is called quieter because it works through demand rather than through law — a contrast with the legislative measures described just before.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 attributes to consumers a financing role the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 3 confuses buyers with designers; the passage places design decisions firmly with the firm.

 

• Option 4 invents an opposition between consumers and regulation that the passage does not suggest.

 

NOTE

 

• In “why is X important” questions, look for the effect attributed to X in the passage, not for a reason that merely sounds sensible in the real world.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The chairman insisted that the report is submitted before Friday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. be submitted.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Verbs of command, demand, request, suggestion or insistence — insist, demand, order, suggest, recommend, propose, urge — are followed by a that-clause in the subjunctive mood. The verb in that clause takes its base form for every subject, and the passive is therefore be submitted.
◦ Corrected: The chairman insisted that the report be submitted before Friday.

 

• The base form does not change with the subject or with the tense of the main verb: He insists that she go; He insisted that she go.

 

• In British usage should may be inserted — insisted that the report should be submitted — but the plain subjunctive is the form SSC treats as correct when should is not among the options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘was submitted’ turns the clause into a statement of fact, losing the sense of a demand.

 

• Option 3: ‘will be submitted’ cannot follow a past reporting verb, and the subjunctive takes no future form.

 

• Option 4: ‘has been submitted’ reports a completed action, contradicting before Friday.

 

NOTE

 

• The subjunctive also survives in fixed expressions: It is essential that he be present, I move that the motion be adopted, Long live the king, God bless you, If I were you.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The team performed more better in the second half of the match.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. much better.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Better is already the comparative form of good/well. Placing more before it produces a double comparative, which is ungrammatical in modern English.
◦ Corrected: The team performed much better in the second half of the match.

 

• A comparative is strengthened by much, far, a lot, considerably, rather — never by more.
◦ Example: The second attempt was far easier than the first.

 

• The same rule forbids double superlatives such as most fastest, most best or most worst.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘more good’ is wrong because good forms its comparative irregularly — good → better → best.

 

• Option 3: ‘far more better’ keeps the double comparative and merely adds another intensifier.

 

• Option 4: ‘more well’ is equally faulty; well also becomes better.

 

NOTE

 

• Irregular degrees worth memorising: good/well – better – best, bad/badly – worse – worst, little – less – least, much/many – more – most, far – farther/further – farthest/furthest.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to me, “I shall meet you here tomorrow.”
option_1: He told me that he shall meet me here tomorrow.
option_2: He told me that he would meet me there the next day.
option_3: He told me that he will meet me there the next day.
option_4: He told me that he would have met me there tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He told me that he would meet me there the next day.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Four changes are required here:
◦ the reporting verb said to me becomes told me;
◦ the pronoun I becomes he, and you becomes me;
◦ the modal shall is back-shifted to would;
◦ the adverbs of place and time change: here → there and tomorrow → the next day.

 

• Indirect: He told me that he would meet me there the next day.

 

• Note that shall/will both become would in reported speech when the reporting verb is in the past.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves shall, here and tomorrow untouched.

 

• Option 3 changes the adverbs but not the modal, keeping will after a past reporting verb.

 

• Option 4 uses would have met, which suggests an action that never happened.

 

NOTE

 

• Standard adverb changes: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, here → there, this → that, ago → before, next week → the following week.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

She told me that she had been waiting since morning.
option_1: “I had been waiting since morning,” she told me.
option_2: “I have been waiting since morning,” she told me.
option_3: “She has been waiting since morning,” she told me.
option_4: “I am waiting since morning,” she told me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. “I have been waiting since morning,” she told me.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In reported speech the past reporting verb told had pushed the tense one step back. Converting to direct speech, that back-shift must be undone: the past perfect continuous had been waiting returns to the present perfect continuous have been waiting.

 

• The pronoun she becomes I, since the speaker now speaks in her own voice, and the sentence is enclosed in inverted commas with a capital letter at the start.
◦ Direct: “I have been waiting since morning,” she told me.

 

• The preposition since with a point of time correctly demands a perfect continuous form, which confirms the choice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the back-shifted past perfect continuous, so the conversion has not been made.

 

• Option 3 leaves the reported pronoun she inside the quotation, which no speaker would say of herself.

 

• Option 4 uses the present continuous with since, which is grammatically wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• Reverse back-shift while converting to direct speech: past → present, past perfect → present perfect or simple past, past perfect continuous → present perfect continuous, would → will, could → can, might → may.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. For three winters the farmers had complained that the canal ran dry weeks before the sowing season.

 

A. The engineers who inspected it found no leak in the lining and no fault in the gates.

 

B. A retired schoolmaster pointed out that the fields at the head of the canal had lately taken to a thirstier crop.

 

C. Once the sowing was staggered by a fortnight, water reached the tail-end fields again.

 

D. Readings taken through the following season confirmed his explanation.

 

S2. The canal had not been failing; it had merely been asked to do more than before.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-B-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – B – D – C – S2, and the paragraph follows an investigation order: complaint → examination → hypothesis → confirmation → remedy → conclusion.

 

• S1 states the complaint.
◦ A is the first response to it — the engineers inspect it, the pronoun pointing back to the canal, and rule out the obvious causes.
◦ B offers the alternative explanation, which is worth stating only after the mechanical faults in A have been ruled out.
◦ D follows immediately, because “his explanation” can refer only to the schoolmaster in B.
◦ C gives the remedy that the confirmed explanation makes possible, and leads into the verdict in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) allows the explanation to be offered before anyone has examined the canal, and separates B from D.

 

• Option 3 (A-D-B-C) places “his explanation” before the person whose explanation it is has been mentioned.

 

• Option 4 (B-D-A-C) pushes the engineers’ inspection to a point where it no longer serves any purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• A possessive pronoun (his, her, its, their) is the strongest link in such questions: the sentence containing it must follow the sentence that names the person or thing it stands for.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Cinnamon was once among the most closely guarded secrets of the ancient spice trade.

 

A. Merchants who controlled the supply encouraged the tale instead of correcting it.

 

B. Greek writers solemnly recorded that the bark was carried by great birds to nests on cliffs no man could climb.

 

C. Only when European ships reached the coast of Sri Lanka did the truth become plain.

 

D. The mystery kept prices high and rivals away for several centuries.

 

S2. The spice was not rare at all; it grew in abundance on perfectly ordinary trees.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. B-A-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – D – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from secret → the story that guarded it → who profited by it → the effect → the exposure.

 

• S1 announces the secret.
◦ B supplies the fantastic story that served as the secret’s cover, and must come first because the later sentences all refer back to it.
◦ A speaks of “the tale”, a definite article pointing straight to the story told in B.
◦ D states the consequence — high prices and absent rivals — which follows once merchants had propagated the tale.
◦ C brings the end of the deception (Only when … did the truth become plain), leading directly into the revelation in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (A-B-D-C) opens with “the tale” before any tale has been told.

 

• Option 3 (B-D-A-C) separates A from B, leaving the merchants’ encouragement stranded after its consequence.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-A-C) begins with the effect of a mystery that has not yet been described.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the definite article: a phrase such as the tale, the change, the mystery refers to something already introduced, so that sentence can never stand first among the jumbled ones.
